explanations: terra: East and west belong to God and whichever way people turn there is God's face, setting a divine boundary around the merely directional turning rejected as righteousness in 2:177.

luna: The section joins turning the face, giving wealth, freeing necks, truthfulness, and piety; this verse assembles those same acts, while saying outwardly turning the face east or west is not itself righteousness. | terra: The ayah denies that righteousness is merely turning faces, then defines it through giving loved wealth, freeing necks, truthfulness, and taqwa; it is the section's face, hand, release, affirmation, and shield in one definition.
luna: The section says the giver has no human favor to repay and seeks the Lord's face; this verse casts spending as a good loan to God, who multiplies it, making the ultimate return divine.

luna: The section says no human favor can be repaid and worldly wealth will not save its owner; this verse calls people to spend before a Day with no bargaining, friendship, or intercession, directly joining giving to the limit of earthly ties.

luna: The section's high garden yields double fruit after a downpour; this verse uses seed that multiplies manyfold as a likeness for spending in God's way, linking giving to fruitful increase. | terra: Spending in God's way is likened to a grain producing seven multiplied ears, another concrete picture of a giving act becoming growth.

luna: The section's giver seeks God's face without asking people for return; this verse forbids following charity with reminders or injury and promises reward without fear, distinguishing the open hand from a self-serving one. | terra: Those who spend without reminder or injury have reward and no fear, identifying the conduct whose fertile image follows in 2:265.
luna: The section's true giver refuses to seek thanks; this verse says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, clarifying what makes giving fit for the sought face.

luna: The section contrasts the high garden that flourishes after rain with the falling ravine; this verse's charity-for-show is like soil washed off bare rock by rain, a precise reversal where the gift leaves no lasting fruit. | terra: Charity spoiled by reminders, injury, and display is a thin covering of soil swept from a rock by rain, the barren rain-scene against the high garden that doubles its fruit.

luna: The section quotes the high garden hit by a downpour and yielding double fruit; this verse stages that scene and ties its abundance to spending in search of God's approval. | terra: Spending for God's approval is a garden on high ground whose rain yields double produce, directly uniting giving, sought approval, height, rain, and growth.

luna: The section's high garden bears abundant fruit after rain; this neighboring garden parable imagines destructive weather striking an owner who is old and has vulnerable children, making the fruitful garden's security a consequential contrast. | terra: A fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its aged owner most needs it, bringing garden, lost provision, and fire together as the vulnerable reverse of enduring giving.
terra: Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty, identifying the competing promises behind a hand that either closes or gives.

luna: The source section's wording وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ in 92:20 names the giver's sought face; this verse says charity is for seeking Allah's face (لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ) and its full reward, making the refusal of human repayment a positive aim. | terra: Spending is to be done only in seeking God's face, and whatever is spent is repaid in full; this directly clarifies the section's giving for the face without seeking repayment from recipients.

luna: The section opens with night covering and day appearing, then divides human striving; this verse names people who give by night and day, in secret and in public, and promises them security, joining the time-image to the giving path. | terra: Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and openly, join the surah's opening times to its giving hand and receive their reward from their Lord.
terra: The wealth and children of the disbelievers avail nothing against God and they become fuel for fire, joining failed possession to the blaze.

luna: The section sets the Lord who gives against Pharaoh's claim to be the highest ruler; this verse says sovereignty is God's to grant or take away, and honor or abase, exposing the king's claimed height as borrowed and temporary.

luna: The section opens with night covering and day appearing, then speaks of the Lord who creates and gives; this verse joins night entering day with bringing life from death and providing without measure, meeting those images in one statement.

luna: The section describes wealth given for God's face; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, clarifying the cost and quality of the open hand. | terra: Righteousness cannot be attained until one spends from what one loves, concentrating the same bond between loved wealth and true goodness that 2:177 supplies to the section.

luna: The section joins a brink, divine favor, rescue, and guidance; this verse says the believers stood at the edge of a pit of Fire, were rescued from it, and became brothers, making communal reconciliation another form of grace that turns people from the brink. | terra: God's favor makes former enemies brothers and rescues them from the brink of a pit of fire; brink, rescue, favor, and guidance occupy one scene exactly as the section describes.
terra: The audience is told to race toward forgiveness and a vast garden prepared for those with taqwa, joining urgent movement, shield, and garden.
terra: The people of taqwa spend in prosperity and adversity, restrain anger, and pardon, specifying the giving conduct that leads to that garden.

luna: The section opposes giving to hoarding; this verse uses the source-section root ب خ ل for those who withhold what God gave them and says it will be wrapped around their necks, turning retained wealth into a fitting burden. | terra: What people withhold from God's bounty will be collared around their necks, while the inheritance of heaven and earth belongs to God; gripped wealth becomes its owner's grip and divine ownership remains.

luna: The section's miser is marked by the root ب خ ل; this verse names those who are miserly and hide God's bounty, pairing the same withholding with concealment. | terra: Those who are stingy, command stinginess, and conceal what God gave from His bounty combine the clenched hand with denial of the original Giver.
terra: One who turns from the Messenger after guidance is clear and follows another path is left to that choice and burned in Hell, joining turning, divided way, and fire.
terra: The claim that God's hand is fettered is reversed by the declaration that His hands are outspread and He spends as He wills, directly opposing the clenched hand to the giving Lord.
terra: The Prophet is told not to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening desiring His face; their mutual accounts are not one another's burden.
terra: God's straight path is to be followed rather than the several paths that divide their walkers, making the section's diverging courses an explicit command.
terra: Those who deny God's signs and act arrogantly cannot enter the garden, an impossible ascent image that bars self-exaltation from the high garden.
terra: The garden-dwellers praise God for guiding them there and say they could not have found guidance without Him, carrying divine guidance to the garden outcome.

luna: The section's branded miser is introduced by this warning against hoarding gold and silver without spending in God's way; the next verse supplies the brand, while this one identifies the stored wealth and refusal. | terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend in God's way are warned of punishment, identifying the withheld wealth that becomes branding metal in 9:35.

luna: The section contrasts the pious person kept from harm with the hoarder whose flanks are branded; this verse makes the held gold and silver into the heated iron that brands forehead, sides, and back. | terra: Hoarded treasure is heated in Hell and brands foreheads, flanks, and backs, making wealth cling as fire to the very face, side, and turned back of its keeper.
terra: The hypocrites command wrong, forbid right, and close their hands; forgetting God follows the same bodily posture of refusal the section gives to the miser.

luna: The section opposes giving to withholding; this man promises لَنَصَّدَّقَنَّ if given from God's bounty, using the same giving root ء ت ي as source-section 92:18 يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ. | terra: A person vows that if God gives from His bounty, he will certainly give charity and be righteous, tying divine giving to the human promise to give.

luna: The section describes one who clutches wealth and turns his back; after receiving bounty, these people become miserly and turn away, repeating the source-section's give/withhold and turn-away pattern. | terra: After God gives them from His bounty, they become stingy with it and turn away, the exact reversal of the giver who confirms the good and directs his face toward God.

luna: The section says their vow and later conduct put giving and turning away in one story; this continuation says breaking the promise and lying leaves hypocrisy in their hearts, naming the lasting consequence of that reversal. | terra: Broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the day they meet God, continuing the consequence of receiving bounty, withholding it, and turning away.

luna: The section contrasts a structure founded on taqwa with one that collapses into Hell; this verse identifies the opposing mosque built for harm, disbelief, and division, supplying the bad intention behind the unstable foundation in the next ayah.

luna: The section sets the ravine-edge building against one founded on taqwa and seeking God's approval; this neighboring verse explicitly says the mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy, completing the positive side of the contrast.

luna: The section puts the high garden of taqwa against a structure on a ravine's edge that collapses into Hell; this verse depicts exactly that unstable foundation and fall, marking the boundary between the two builds. | terra: A building founded on taqwa and God's approval is set against one on a collapsing cliff-edge that falls with its builder into Hell, the section's shielded height and fiery abyss in one comparison.
terra: God purchases believers' lives and wealth in exchange for the garden and names His promise true, uniting wealth given away, divine covenant, and garden return.
terra: God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, joining the palace greeting for the follower of guidance to its final destination.
terra: Those seeking their Lord's face persist, pray, spend secretly and openly, and repel evil with good, placing the face sought and the giving act within one steadfast course.
luna: The section contrasts a stable garden with a structure that collapses; this parable describes a good word as a good tree with a firm root, giving another image of grounded growth.
luna: The section's garden receives rain and yields doubled fruit; this continuation says the good tree gives fruit continually by its Lord's leave, echoing durable yield.
luna: The section contrasts the secure garden with a ravine-edge structure that falls; this paired parable sets the bad word as a tree uprooted from the earth without stability.
terra: The guilty wear garments of pitch while fire covers their faces, a bodily reversal of wealth worn like a garment and the face opened by divine protection.
terra: God declares that the direction of the path rests upon Him while some paths deviate, a close formulation of divine guidance amid the section's forked road.
luna: The section says night veils human striving and day reveals it; this verse calls night and day signs and makes the visible day a means of seeking bounty and counting time.

luna: The section contrasts the one who clings to worldly property with the one who trusts lasting reward; this verse says whoever wants the immediate life is given some of it and then faces Hell. | terra: Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and then reaches Hell condemned, making divine giving itself no proof of final height.

luna: The section's giver strives for the Lord's pleasure; this verse pairs desire for the Hereafter with the striving appropriate to it. | terra: Whoever wants the Hereafter, strives for it properly, and believes has that striving thanked, joining direction of desire to the value of effort.

luna: The section's palace dialogue distinguishes the Lord who provides from the king who claims dominion; this verse says God's bounty reaches both groups, adding that worldly provision alone does not mark the final path. | terra: God supplies both groups from His giving and His giving is not confined, establishing the open divine hand before the roads reach different ends.
terra: Worldly ranks differ, but the Hereafter has greater degrees and preference, relocating true elevation beyond present possessions.
terra: The command pictures a hand chained to the neck or spread without limit, giving the section's held and opened hands a bodily measure rather than treating either posture abstractly.

luna: The section contrasts God as giver with human reluctance to release wealth; this verse says that even owners of the treasuries of their Lord's mercy would hold back for fear of spending, making the human grip the counter-image to God's provision.
terra: He is told to remain with those seeking their Lord's face morning and evening and not turn his eyes toward worldly adornment, joining face, turning, and the pull of possessions.

luna: The section centers on a man recalling his worldly companion; this garden owner boasts to his companion of having more wealth and stronger support, staging a close counterpart to the proud worldly bond. | terra: The garden owner boasts to his believing companion that he has more wealth and a stronger following, joining possession, social power, and companionship.
terra: He enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, treating fertile possession as permanent support.

luna: The section's companion mocks belief and resurrection; this garden owner says he does not think the Hour will come, making the same disbelief concrete in a second companion scene. | terra: He doubts the Hour and assumes that even if returned to his Lord he will find a better resort, making denial and self-sufficiency speak inside the garden.

luna: The section contrasts the Lord's giving with a person's pride; the companion here answers by recalling creation from dust and a drop, redirecting wealth-boasting to the Creator. | terra: His companion answers by recalling the God who created him from dust and a drop, confronting denial with the Creator just as Moses confronts Pharaoh.

luna: The section's giver seeks the face of the Lord above; this companion declares his Lord is Allah and refuses association, opposing the garden owner's self-confidence. | terra: The believer declares God his Lord and refuses to associate anyone with Him, providing the companion's affirmation against the owner's boast.
terra: He tells the owner to acknowledge God's will and that power belongs only to God when entering the garden, locating the true supporting hand over the apparent wealth.
terra: The believer warns that his Lord may give him a better garden and send a calamity that turns the other's garden into barren ground, bringing divine giving and garden reversal together.
terra: He warns that its water may sink beyond recovery, making the garden's apparent provision fall out of the owner's reach.

luna: The section says wealth will not avail when its owner falls; this garden owner's crop is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, showing worldly possession collapsing. | terra: A garden owner's fruit is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while its trellises lie fallen, a secondary garden-and-collapse scene where possession cannot hold up its owner.

luna: The section's worldly companion cannot truly secure his friend; this verse says the garden owner has no group to help him apart from God, exposing the limit of human backing. | terra: He has no company to help him apart from God and cannot save himself, clarifying the absence of a human hand at the moment wealth and garden fail.

luna: The section's rescue and favor belong to the Lord; after the garden's ruin, this verse says true protection and reward belong to God, resolving the companion story on that basis. | terra: In that collapsed-garden scene, true protection belongs to God and His outcome is best, returning support and final result to the divine owner.

luna: The section sets a fire approached for guidance against the Fire entered by the heedless; Musa says he may find guidance at the fire (هُدًى), making the approached fire a sign rather than a punishment. | terra: Moses sees a fire during the night and hopes to find guidance at it, directly presenting the fire read from a safe distance as a sign along the road.

luna: The section says Musa's fire is approached as a source of guidance; this continuation has him arrive at the fire and hear the call that begins divine instruction. | terra: When Moses reaches the fire he is called by name, supplying the voice at the end of the night approach anticipated in 20:10.

luna: The section's guiding fire leads Musa to a message; this call marks the ground as sacred and directs him to remove his sandals, showing the encounter's reverent threshold. | terra: At the fire the voice identifies itself as Moses' Lord and marks the valley as sacred, confirming that the approached flame is the site of divine address.

luna: The section's fire is the scene where guidance is found; this continuation says God chose Musa and orders him to listen, identifying the guidance received there. | terra: God tells Moses that he has been chosen and must listen to revelation, giving the night-fire its guiding function through heard speech.

luna: The section makes the fire an occasion of warning and orientation; Musa is told here that God is his Lord and to establish prayer for His remembrance. | terra: The speaker at the fire declares Himself God and commands worship and remembrance, fixing the true Lord before Moses later faces Pharaoh's competing claim.
terra: At the fire God says the Hour is coming and partly concealed so that every soul is repaid for what it strives, joining hiddenness, striving, and repayment.
terra: Moses is warned not to let one who denies the Hour and follows desire turn him from it and bring him to ruin, echoing the companion who nearly ruins the believer.
terra: God sends Moses and Aaron together to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, establishing the two messengers and the king in the palace encounter.
terra: They are commanded to speak gently so Pharaoh may remember or fear, showing that the warning seeks the very fear that would protect him.
terra: The two confess fear that Pharaoh will hasten against them or transgress further, making royal force part of the confrontation with divine guidance.
terra: God tells them not to fear because He is with them hearing and seeing, supplying the divine support beneath the hands sent before the king.

luna: The section sets Musa and Harun before Pharaoh and gives them a greeting of peace for the one who follows guidance (السَّلَامُ عَلَى مَنِ اتَّبَعَ الْهُدَى); this is the first half of the encounter where guidance and turning away divide outcomes. | terra: Moses and Aaron are taught to tell Pharaoh that peace belongs to the one who follows guidance, opening the palace encounter with the section's offered path.

luna: The section links 92:16's denial and turning away to the opposite of the guided path; Musa and Harun's warning here places punishment on whoever denies and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ). | terra: Their message assigns punishment to whoever denies and turns away, bringing the two acts of 92:16 into the same confrontation with Pharaoh.

luna: The section frames the palace encounter as a contest over who gives and rules; Pharaoh's question, “Who is your Lord?”, makes that disputed lordship explicit before Musa answers. | terra: Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron who their Lord is; the question stages the contest between the king who claims lordship and the Lord who gives.

luna: The section says Musa's answer gathers the surah's creating, giving, and guiding into one statement; this verse says the Lord gave each thing its created form and then guided it, bringing those acts together against Pharaoh's claim. | terra: Moses answers that their Lord gave every thing its created form and then guided it, joining creation, giving, and guidance in the single divine action highlighted by the section.

luna: The section says Musa's answer gathers creation, giving, and guidance; this continuation of the answer names the Lord who makes the earth a resting place, lays paths through it, sends water, and brings out plants, illustrating provision and direction.
luna: The section's palace answer identifies the Lord as giver; this next verse tells people to eat and pasture their livestock from what God has provided, making the provision concrete.

luna: The section's palace encounter contrasts God's guidance with denial and turning away; after Musa's answer, this verse says Pharaoh was shown every sign but denied them and refused, repeating the denial root ك ذ ب.
terra: God guides Moses to lead His servants by night and strike a dry path through the sea without fear of pursuit or drowning, turning guidance into a safe road at the edge of destruction.
terra: Pharaoh follows with his forces and the sea overwhelms them, giving the self-exalting king the downward outcome avoided by the guided walkers.
terra: Pharaoh is judged to have led his people astray rather than guided them, directly opposing the holding king's leadership to the Lord who gives and guides.
terra: The disbelievers cannot ward the fire from their faces or backs and receive no help, reversing God's shielding of the givers and recalling the branded front and back.
terra: Those for whom God's best has preceded are kept far from Hell, a direct counterpart to the God-fearing giver being moved to its side rather than entering it.
terra: They do not even hear Hell and remain in what their souls desire, defining the safe distance that separates sign from burning presence.
terra: The question asks who holds sovereignty over everything, protecting while none can protect against Him; hand-like ownership and the section's shield meet in one divine prerogative.
terra: The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger, joining hands, regret, and the road missed.
terra: He wishes he had not taken a particular person as an intimate friend, matching the section's remembered companion who nearly caused his fall.
terra: That friend led him away from remembrance after it reached him, explaining how companionship turns a person from the warning-sign.
luna: The section gives night and day opposite roles in the divided course of life; this verse pairs night as covering and sleep as rest with day as a time of rising.
terra: The Messenger asks no payment for warning except that a person choose a path to the Lord, joining refusal of return to the road the hearer takes.
terra: The servants of the Merciful spend neither wastefully nor stingily but hold a measured course, giving the opened hand a disciplined middle position.
terra: On the judgment day neither wealth nor children benefit, establishing the boundary at which possession ceases to be a saving hand.

luna: The section explicitly connects the root ص ل ي in source-section 92:15's يَصْلَىٰهَا with this fire Musa approaches to warm himself (تَصْطَلُونَ); the shared root makes one fire warm at a safe distance and the other burn when entered. | terra: Moses tells his family that the fire may yield news or a burning brand so they can warm themselves; its form of the ṣ-l-y root makes nearness to fire warming here where entering Hell burns.

luna: The section contrasts an approached sign-fire with the Fire of punishment; at Musa's fire this verse announces blessing for those present, completing the welcoming rather than punishing side. | terra: On reaching the fire Moses hears a blessing upon those at and around it and God's transcendence proclaimed, continuing the fire-as-revelatory-sign scene.

luna: The section says the fire-path yields guidance; this continuation identifies the caller as Allah, the Mighty and Wise, making the source of that guidance explicit. | terra: The voice at the fire tells Moses that it is God, the Mighty and Wise, explicitly identifying the giver of the sign and guidance.

luna: The section develops Musa's family traveling at night and his hope of finding fire or guidance; this verse repeats the journey, the distant fire, and his instruction to the family to wait. | terra: Moses sees a fire after completing his term and tells his family he may bring news or a brand so they may warm themselves, a full parallel to the guiding night-fire.

luna: The section uses Musa's fire as a source of direction; this continuation calls to him from the tree in the blessed valley, where he receives the divine address. | terra: When Moses reaches the fire he is called from the blessed spot, showing that the approached sign carries a divine voice rather than consuming him.
terra: Pharaoh tells his chiefs he knows no god for them but himself and orders a tower built so he can ascend, making self-claimed lordship and manufactured height oppose Moses' giving Lord.
terra: God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea, bringing the claimant of height under the stronger divine taking hand.
terra: Qarun exalts himself over Moses' people while treasure keys burden a strong company, staging wealth as both claimed height and physical weight.
terra: He is told to seek the final abode with what God gave him, do good as God did good to him, and avoid corruption, directing received wealth toward its Giver and the last life.
terra: Qarun claims he received his wealth because of knowledge he possesses, replacing divine bounty with self-sufficient possession even after stronger wealthy peoples were destroyed.
terra: He comes out in adornment and those desiring the near life wish for wealth like his, showing possession attracting faces toward worldly height.
terra: Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better for believers who do right, redirecting desire from displayed wealth toward the lasting return.
terra: God makes the earth swallow Qarun and his house; no company helps him against God and he cannot save himself, an exceptionally close meeting of wealth, fall, absent hand, and ruin.
terra: Those who had desired Qarun's place recognize that God expands and measures provision and that His favor kept them from being swallowed, turning envy into acknowledgment of saving bounty.
terra: The final abode is for those who do not desire exaltation or corruption on earth, drawing the boundary between the sought Most High and Pharaoh's desire to be high.
terra: Everything perishes except God's face, and judgment and return belong to Him; this gives ultimate duration and ownership to the face sought by the giver.

luna: The section says the giving hand seeks the Lord's face rather than human repayment; this verse commands giving relatives, needy people, and travelers their due, calling that better for those seeking God's face. | terra: Giving the due of kin, the needy, and the traveler is declared good for those who desire God's face, joining directed wealth and the sought face.

luna: The section contrasts human repayment with the Lord's lasting reward; this verse says wealth gained through usury does not grow with God, while charity seeking His face is multiplied. | terra: Riba given to grow within people's wealth does not grow with God, while zakat given seeking His face makes its givers the multipliers; it joins face, giving, purification, and true increase.
terra: Those who pray and spend secretly and openly hope for a trade that will never perish, directing transient wealth toward what remains.
terra: God fully repays them and increases them from His bounty, joining recompense and increase to the giving that sought an imperishable return.
terra: The children of Adam are reminded of God's covenant not to serve Satan, the clear enemy, placing the warning before the divided path.
terra: Serving God is identified as the straight path, making the response to warning a road rather than an abstract assent.
terra: Satan has led many generations astray, a broad counterpart to the companion who nearly draws the believer into ruin.
terra: The warned are shown the Hell they were promised, bringing promise, warning, and fire to the point of encounter.
terra: They are commanded to enter and burn in it because they denied, directly joining denial to entry into the warning-fire.
terra: The dominion of everything is in God's hand and all are returned to Him, a direct answer to every human attempt to hold wealth or kingdom.

luna: The section recounts a man speaking about his worldly companion; this verse introduces that remembered companion and supplies the human bond on which the later warning turns. | terra: A garden-dweller says he had a companion, establishing the worldly relationship whose mockery and near-ruin the following ayat recall.

luna: The section's worldly companion mocks the believer for affirming resurrection; this companion asks whether the speaker believes they will be judged (أَئِنَّكَ لَمِنَ الْمُصَدِّقِينَ), making denial the first edge of the later rescue scene. | terra: The garden-dweller recalls his companion mocking him for affirming resurrection; this supplies the personal act of denial behind the section's companion, fall, and fire meeting.

luna: The section quotes the companion's mockery in 37:52; this next question spells out its resurrection-denial, explaining why seeing him in the Fire answers the very claim he mocked. | terra: The mocking companion asks whether dust and bones will really be judged after death, specifying the denial recalled in 37:52 before the downward look into Hell.

luna: The section's man looks down to see his former companion; this question, هل أنتم مطلعون, is the scene's invitation to look and directly sets up that downward sight. | terra: He asks the other people of the garden whether they will look down, introducing the deliberate high-to-low gaze realized in 37:55.

luna: The section's believer looks down and sees his former companion in the middle of Hell; this ayah narrates that very look and sight (فَاطَّلَعَ فَرَآهُ فِي سَوَاءِ الْجَحِيمِ). | terra: The saved man looks down and sees his former companion in the midst of Hell, directly joining height, downward sight, and the fire below.

luna: The section says his friend nearly rolled him into ruin; the speaker says كِدْتَ لَتُرْدِينِ, from the same root ر د ي as source-section 92:11 تَرَدَّى, linking the friend's influence to the later plunge. | terra: He tells the companion that he nearly brought him to ruin, making another person's pull toward a fall part of the fire scene.

luna: The section contrasts no human favor owed with one saving grace from the Lord; here the saved man says his Lord's favor kept him from being brought to punishment, making divine grace the hinge of the cliff-and-Fire scene. | terra: The speaker attributes his absence from Hell solely to his Lord's favor, which sharpens the section's distinction between an unrepaid human favor and the saving divine favor.

luna: After the section's account of rescue from the Fire, the speaker asks whether they are not dead; this begins the rescued believers' reflection on the outcome their companion denied. | terra: The garden speaker asks whether the saved will die again, continuing his amazed recognition that favor has removed him from the companion's fiery outcome.

luna: The section sets a denier's fate against the Lord's saving favor; this continuation says their only death was the first and they are not being punished, completing the contrast in their own words. | terra: He excepts only the first death and asks whether punishment is now absent, helping specify the lasting safety supplied by divine favor.

luna: The section makes rescue from the Fire depend on the Lord's favor; the next declaration calls this the great triumph, naming the consequence of that rescue. | terra: He names this rescue the great attainment, giving the garden-side outcome of the section's divergent striving.

luna: The section ends with the one who sought the Lord's face attaining contentment; this continuation tells hearers to work toward the just-described triumph, linking the scene to the surah's divergent striving. | terra: The command that workers should work for such an outcome links the companion scene back to the surah's claim that human striving is diverse.
terra: A condemned person must shield his face from the worst punishment, a grim reversal of God shielding those who gave for His face.
terra: The one who brings truth and the one who confirms it are identified as the people of taqwa, joining affirmation to the section's protective stance.
terra: They have whatever they desire with their Lord, and that is the reward of those who do good, carrying affirmation and taqwa into divine recompense.
luna: The section opposes the one who turns away from warning to the one kept from Fire; this verse describes the deniers with blackened faces on Resurrection Day and names Hell as their home.

luna: The section says the God-fearing are kept away from the Fire; this verse says God saves those who feared Him and evil does not touch them, giving the protective side of the contrast. | terra: God saves those who had taqwa by their attainment so that evil does not touch or grieve them, another explicit realization of taqwa as a shield.
terra: On resurrection the whole earth is in God's grasp and the heavens folded in His right hand, making the supporting and possessing divine hand cosmic in scope.
terra: Pharaoh orders Haman to build him a tower so he may reach the ways, turning the king's claim of height into an attempted structure.
terra: He says he will ascend toward Moses' God while calling Moses a liar, and his scheme bars him from the path and ends in ruin; height, denial, path, and collapse meet here.
terra: Pharaoh's people are exposed to fire morning and evening and then ordered into harsher punishment when the Hour comes, fixing the final fire beneath their worldly elevation.

terra: Whoever seeks the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase in it, while one seeking the worldly harvest receives some of it but no share later; desire, growth, and first-last choice divide one ayah.

luna: The section opposes the Lord who gives to Pharaoh as a king who holds dominion; Pharaoh boasts of Egypt and its rivers as possessions, making earthly rule his counterclaim. | terra: Pharaoh proclaims the kingdom of Egypt his and points to rivers beneath him, giving the section's holding king a concrete boast of property and elevation.
luna: The section contrasts divine giving with a king's self-exaltation; Pharaoh follows his boast by belittling Musa as weak and unclear, showing how the claim is used against the messenger.
luna: The section exposes the king's confusion of wealth with true elevation; Pharaoh asks why Musa lacks gold bracelets and angelic company, treating possessions as proof of rank.
terra: Pharaoh makes light of his people and they obey him, showing how the king's claimed elevation draws others onto his course.
terra: When they provoke God's anger He takes retribution and drowns them all, completing the fall beneath the king's earlier boast over rivers.
terra: The people of the garden taste no death beyond the first, and God protects them from Hell, extending the rescued garden-dweller's reflection on death and fire.
terra: That protection is explicitly a bounty from the Lord and the great success, closely paralleling the saved companion's appeal to his Lord's favor.

luna: The section divides the giver from the one who is miserly; this verse says those who withhold only withhold from themselves, clarifying the cost of holding back. | terra: Those summoned to spend include one who is stingy only against himself; God is self-sufficient while humans are needy, directly reversing the miser's claim to independence.
terra: God's hand is over the hands of those who pledge; breaking the pledge harms oneself, while fulfilling it receives a great reward, joining hand, promise, and divine support.
terra: The people of the garden receive what their Lord gives them because they previously did good, reversing the direction of giving at the garden's reward.
terra: Within their wealth is an acknowledged right for the asker and deprived, making the giving hand part of the conduct that precedes the garden.
terra: The people of the garden rejoice in what their Lord gave them and in His protection from Hell, joining divine giving, garden joy, and shielding from fire.
terra: The Hereafter and the first life belong to God, nearly restating the ownership claim by which the section brings down Pharaoh's supremacy.
luna: The section contrasts a king's temporary claim to elevation with God's lasting dominion; this verse says everyone on earth passes away, establishing what cannot remain.

luna: The source section's wording وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ (92:20) makes the sought divine face central; this verse says the face of the Lord remains, joining that face to the passage's contrast between what passes and what endures. | terra: The face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains, supporting the section's direction of transient wealth toward the enduring divine face.

luna: The section treats Musa's fire as useful and warning fire at once; this question begins another Quranic reflection on fire by asking about what people kindle. | terra: The audience is asked to consider the fire it kindles, shifting attention from Hell alone to an actual humanly approached fire.

luna: The section says an approached fire may warm and guide; this verse asks whether people created its tree or God did, placing useful fire within divine provision. | terra: God asks whether humans made its tree or He did, returning even the usable fire to the Lord who creates and gives each thing its capacity.

luna: The section's fire is a sign on the night path; this verse calls fire a reminder and provision for travelers, directly meeting the signal and usefulness in the image. | terra: God made that fire a reminder and a provision for travelers, almost exactly the section's fire serving as warning-sign and help on a night road.
terra: God is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, adding divine permanence and disclosed-hidden polarity to His ownership of the first and later life.
luna: The section's rejected human repayment is paired with seeking the Lord's approval; this verse likewise asks who will lend God a good loan and promises its multiplication.
terra: Charitable men and women who extend a good loan to God receive multiplication and a noble reward, joining purification-like charity, increase, and divine return.

luna: The section's garden rises and produces, while its final reward outlasts worldly possession; this verse's rain-grown vegetation pleases briefly before drying and crumbling, clarifying how worldly abundance can pass.
terra: Those who are stingy and command stinginess are warned that whoever turns away cannot diminish God, the self-sufficient and praiseworthy, joining withholding, turning, and true independence.
terra: Neither wealth nor children avail against God, and their possessors are companions of the fire, directly bounding wealth's ability to save.

luna: The section contrasts the hand that gives with the one that is miserly and describes brothers; this verse praises people who prefer others over themselves and says whoever is protected from stinginess of soul succeeds, directly meeting both motifs. | terra: The Helpers prefer others even while in need, and protection from the self's avarice marks success, joining generous preference with the shield against grasping.

luna: The section uses the rescued believers' brotherhood as a sign of grace; this continuation has later believers ask that their hearts be free of rancor toward those who came before, extending that reconciled bond.
terra: The hypocrites urge others to stop spending on the Messenger's companions so they disperse, although the treasuries of heaven and earth belong to God; withholding confronts divine ownership.
terra: Believers are warned not to let wealth and children turn them from God's remembrance, identifying possession itself as a possible agent of turning.

luna: The section says wealth cannot help once its owner falls; this verse has the dying person ask for a brief delay so he can give charity and become righteous, showing the moment when withheld time and wealth can no longer be recovered. | terra: They are told to spend before death makes a person beg for time to give charity and become righteous, showing the giving hand recognized too late.
luna: The section places the failure of wealth at the moment of falling; this continuation says God does not delay a soul when its appointed time comes, completing the urgency of the preceding plea.
terra: Fear God, listen, obey, and spend; whoever is protected from the avarice of the self prospers, so giving, taqwa, and a protective barrier against inner stinginess stand together.
terra: God makes a way out for whoever has taqwa, giving the section's protective fear a literal opening in the road.
terra: He provides from an unexpected direction and suffices the one who trusts Him, while setting a measure for everything; provision, true sufficiency, and measure meet here.
terra: Blessed is the One in whose hand is dominion and who has power over everything, directly opposing divine possession and support to the king's doomed grasp.
terra: Those who disbelieve in their Lord receive Hell, the evil destination that begins the surah's warning interrogation.
terra: When cast into it they hear it roaring as it boils, making entry into fire the opposite of hearing guidance beside Moses' fire.
terra: Hell's keepers ask each arriving company whether a warner came to them, centering the scene on their treatment of warning.
terra: They admit that a warner came but they denied him, directly explaining why the warning-fire became the entered fire.
terra: They say that listening or reasoning would have kept them from being companions of the blaze, defining the missed act at the sign.
terra: They confess their sin, completing their recognition from within the fire after warning could no longer redirect them.
terra: Those who fear their Lord unseen receive forgiveness and great reward, providing the protected counterpart to those who only recognize the fire after entry.
luna: The section contrasts a fruitful high garden tied to giving with wealth held back; this parable begins with garden owners tested by their crop, another meeting of provision and moral choice.
luna: The section's charitable path releases wealth; these garden owners resolve not to give a share to the poor, making their withheld crop the opposite of the giver's hand.
luna: The section's high garden thrives through rain; this garden is struck by a visitation from the Lord while its owners sleep, turning expected yield into loss.
luna: The section's garden imagery distinguishes flourishing from collapse; this continuation says the crop became like something harvested, completing the loss.

luna: The section's giver directs goods outward; these owners set out saying no poor person should enter the garden, specifying their exclusion. | terra: The garden owners command that no poor person enter their harvest, making a withheld share for the needy the moral cause within the garden scene.

luna: The section's moral hand gives rather than hoards; this verse says the owners go early with the intention of preventing anyone from benefiting, carrying their withholding into action. | terra: They go out confident in their power to withhold, embodying the self-sufficient grasp that the section places on the descending road.

luna: The section's Garden imagery joins abundance to right conduct; after finding the crop destroyed, the owners realize they were deprived, the reversal of their expected abundance. | terra: On seeing the ruined garden they admit they have been deprived, reversing the high garden whose giving yields double fruit.
luna: The section ties abundance to the Lord's gift; this garden's owners confess God's perfection and their own wrongdoing after their plan fails.
luna: The section's giving path seeks the Lord's pleasure; the repentant garden owners hope their Lord will replace the lost crop with something better.
luna: The section contrasts the garden that flourishes with the ravine that falls; this parable closes by naming worldly punishment greater, extending the scene to accountability.
terra: The condemned person says his wealth did not avail him, voicing from inside judgment exactly what the section says the falling miser discovers.
terra: He says his authority has vanished, pairing failed wealth with the loss of claimed power like the king brought down from supremacy.
terra: The command to seize and shackle him replaces the hand that grasped wealth with a stronger hand taking hold of him.
terra: The next command sends the seized man into Hell, completing the movement from useless wealth and fallen authority to entry into fire.

luna: The section's warning Fire divides the two kinds of striving; this verse names the Blaze as the rejected person's end. | terra: The threatened blaze is named immediately before the acts that summon its victim, grounding the following turned back and hoarded wealth in fire rather than in a generic rebuke.

luna: The section places turning away beside entry into the Fire; this continuation describes that Blaze as stripping the scalp, sharpening the warning's consequence. | terra: The blaze strips away the skin, a bodily counterpart to the treasure heated against faces, sides, and backs in the section.

luna: The section repeatedly pairs denial with turning away; this verse says the Fire calls the one who turned back and turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ), echoing the source section's 92:16 تَوَلَّىٰ. | terra: The fire calls the person who turned his back and went away, directly joining fire to the bodily turn of refusal.

luna: The section's miser clutches wealth and finds it cannot help him; this verse adds the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it to those the Fire calls. | terra: That person gathered and withheld, so hoarded wealth and the back turned to warning form one character exactly as in the section.
luna: The section's good hand gives wealth; this verse describes the faithful as assigning a known share of their wealth to the asker and deprived person, specifying the contrary use.
luna: The section's righteous giver directs wealth beyond himself; this line identifies the recipients of that share, the asker and the deprived, completing the contrast with hoarding.
luna: The section's rejected hearer turns his back on the warning; this verse describes a man who turned away and became arrogant, the action immediately preceding his sentence to Saqar.
luna: The section pairs denial and turning away with entry into the Fire; following the arrogant man's rejection, this verse says he will be made to enter Saqar, completing that warning scene.
terra: The fire just described is declared one of the greatest signs, explicitly making fire itself a sign rather than only a destination.
terra: It is a warning to humanity, closely matching the section's warning-fire read as a signal.
terra: The warning addresses whoever chooses to advance or fall back, turning response to the fire-sign into opposed movements.
luna: The section's warning culminates in people entering the Fire; this question names Saqar and invites the condemned to explain how they arrived there.

luna: The section sets the giving, pious person against the one turned away; this answer says the condemned were not among those who prayed, beginning their account of the opposite path. | terra: The people in Saqar confess that they were not among those who prayed, beginning their account of how the fire corresponds to their former stance.

luna: The section's righteous giver gives without repayment; this answer says the condemned did not feed the poor, naming the direct charitable reversal. | terra: They confess that they did not feed the needy, connecting entry into the blaze to the direct opposite of the section's unrecompensed feeding.
luna: The section contrasts truthful warning with denial; this answer says the condemned joined in vain talk, a neighboring account of how they treated the reminder.

luna: The section traces the fire-bound path to denial; this answer says they denied the Day of Recompense, identifying what they rejected. | terra: They confess that they denied the Day of Judgment, joining lack of giving to the denial that elsewhere turns its back on warning.

luna: The section's plunge comes when wealth no longer avails; this answer says the condemned persisted until certainty came, completing their account of delay. | terra: Their denial continued until certainty came, marking the instant when ignored warning became an entered reality.
terra: Faces on that Day are radiant, directly continuing the section's movement from covered night and frowning day to disclosed face.
terra: Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, placing the face's final direction upon the Lord whose face was sought in giving.
terra: God guides the human to the path, after which the person is either grateful or ungrateful, a concise version of one guidance producing two responses.
terra: Chains and a blaze are prepared for the ungrateful, turning one branch of the guided path into entry into fire.
terra: The righteous drink from a prepared cup, beginning the garden-side outcome opposed to the blaze in the preceding ayah.

luna: The section quotes feeding people purely for God's face; this preceding verse shows who receives the food—the needy, orphan, and captive—and that it is given despite being loved. | terra: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own love of food; this identifies the concrete hand and recipients whose purpose is voiced in 76:9.

luna: The section explicitly quotes this declaration of feeding “for the face of Allah” and refusing repayment; its wording لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ and لَا نُرِيدُ مِنكُمْ جَزَاءً matches the source section's hand-and-face meeting. | terra: The feeders say they feed only for God's face and want neither repayment nor thanks, directly joining the giving hand, the sought face, and refusal of human return.

luna: The section's giver acts with fear of the severe Day; this next line gives that fear as the reason for their unreturned feeding. | terra: Their fear of a grim, frowning Day supplies the protective fear behind their unrecompensed giving and makes the threatened day itself wear a face.

luna: The section says the one who fears has a shield and is kept away from evil; this verse says God protected these givers from the evil of that Day, making the shield a concrete act. | terra: God shields them from that Day's evil and grants radiance and joy, completing the section's movement from fearful face and protective giving to an opened face.

luna: The section contrasts the giver's protected path with the Fire and describes a fruitful high garden; this continuation repays patience with a Garden and silk, showing the positive end of giving. | terra: Garden and silk are the reward for the feeders' patience, completing the outcome of the giving, face-seeking, and divine shielding in 76:8-11.
luna: The section's opening night covers people's course; this verse uses the same clothing image, جَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا, making concealment a repeated Quranic scene.
luna: The section pairs covered night with the day that lays striving open; this next verse says daylight is made for livelihood, supplying the contrasting activity.
terra: Moses offers Pharaoh a path to purification, placing the cleansing movement later associated with giving inside the royal confrontation.
terra: He offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he will fear, joining guidance and protective fear in the rejected palace message.
terra: Moses shows Pharaoh the greatest sign, identifying what Pharaoh denies in the next ayah rather than leaving his denial objectless.

luna: The section's rejected warning culminates in denial and turning away; this preceding act says Pharaoh denied the sign and disobeyed, sharing the source-section's denial root ك ذ ب and establishing the choice before his boast. | terra: Pharaoh denies Moses and disobeys, supplying the denial immediately before his turning and boast of supreme lordship.

luna: The section describes turning one's back from warning; this verse says Pharaoh turned away and hurried on (تَوَلَّىٰ), echoing the source section's 92:16 wording for refusal. | terra: He turns away and strives, placing the surah's turning act and its morally divergent striving in the same royal figure.

luna: The section quotes Pharaoh's claim of supreme lordship; this immediately preceding verse has him gather and call out, showing the public act that carries the boast into the encounter. | terra: He gathers the people and calls out, providing the public setting for the claim of height in the next ayah.

luna: The section contrasts the Lord who gives with a king who claims height for himself; Pharaoh's boast أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ reverses the source-section wording رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَىٰ, exposing the king's false claim to the elevation belonging to God. | terra: Pharaoh proclaims himself the highest lord, a direct usurpation of the title belonging to the Lord Most High whose face the giver seeks.

luna: The section says the king who claimed to be highest is brought low; this verse says God seized Pharaoh with punishment in this life and the next, completing the reversal of his boast. | terra: God seizes Pharaoh with the punishment of the latter and the former, answering his claim of supremacy with God's ownership of the last and the first.

luna: The section's warned hearer may read the Fire as a sign and step aside; this story is explicitly called a lesson for whoever fears, clarifying who can receive the warning. | terra: Pharaoh's fate is declared a lesson for whoever fears, turning the palace and punishment scene into the protective fear urged by the section.

luna: The section describes the one who holds to worldly wealth and turns from the warning; this verse names the person who transgresses and prefers the nearer life, identifying the choice behind that refusal. | terra: The one who transgresses begins a compact contrast between self-exaltation and the garden road.

luna: The section contrasts the miser's path with the pious person's; this verse assigns Hell as the abode of the one who prefers worldly life, making the consequence explicit. | terra: Preferring the nearer life makes worldly possession and status the choice opposed to God's ownership of first and last.

luna: The section says the warned person may fear and withdraw from the Fire; this verse describes the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire, the contrary response. | terra: Hell is the refuge for that preference, completing the movement from worldly elevation down to fire.

luna: The section associates fear with being kept away from the Fire; this verse places the self-restrained person's destination in the Garden, completing the opposite outcome to the worldly-life chooser. | terra: The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains desire takes the protective stance opposite Pharaoh and the self-sufficient miser.

luna: The section contrasts two ways and their ends; this closing line names the Garden as the refuge of the one who feared his Lord, finishing the paired warning. | terra: The garden becomes that person's refuge, opposing the high garden of restraint and fear to the fire reached by self-exaltation.
terra: The human being is asked from what God created him, opening a creation-and-road sequence parallel to the section's palace answer.
terra: God creates the human from a drop and measures him, giving created form and measure before the way is eased.
terra: God then eases the way for the human, a direct counterpart to the two ways made easy according to the walker.
terra: Some faces on that Day are bright, another direct formulation of the face opened after the protected course.
terra: Those faces laugh and rejoice, giving emotional content to the final satisfaction promised after striving.
terra: Other faces have dust upon them, reversing radiance with a covering that recalls the road ending in descent.
terra: Darkness covers those faces, making the covering night a judgment image for disbelief rather than the setting through which guidance was read.
terra: The hearers are asked where they are going, forcing attention onto the direction of their course.
terra: The revelation is declared a reminder to all peoples, identifying what can redirect that course.
terra: The reminder is for whoever wills to take a straight course, directly joining warning and road.
terra: Human willing remains under the will of God, Lord of all worlds, returning the walker's road to divine sovereignty.

luna: The section describes divergent striving and a final meeting with the Lord; this verse says each person is laboring toward the Lord and will meet Him, joining effort to the coming judgment. | terra: The human being is laboring toward the Lord and will meet Him, directing all striving toward an unavoidable encounter.

luna: The section's giver is kept from harm and reaches contentment; this verse gives the record in the right hand as the opening sign of the favorable outcome. | terra: The person given his record in his right hand begins the eased outcome of that striving.

luna: The section contrasts ease for one path with difficulty for the other; this verse says the right-handed person will have an easy reckoning, completing the favorable side. | terra: He receives an easy accounting, an eschatological counterpart to being eased toward ease.

luna: The section ends with the saved person attaining satisfaction; this verse's right-handed person returns to his people joyful, a close parallel for that glad outcome. | terra: He returns to his people rejoicing, giving successful striving a satisfied social home.

luna: The section's second path turns its back on warning; this verse places the record behind the back, a concrete image of rejection and opposite fate. | terra: The other person receives his record behind his back, making the turned back the bodily sign of the contrary outcome.

luna: The section says worldly wealth cannot avail the one who falls; after the record is put behind his back, this person cries out for destruction as the account is exposed. | terra: He calls for destruction, recognizing ruin only after taking the back-facing course.

luna: The section contrasts the one kept from Fire with the denier who enters it; this verse sends the back-handed person into a Blaze, completing the same two-outcome pattern. | terra: He enters a blaze, completing the sequence from record behind the back to fire.
terra: He had thought he would never return, identifying denial beneath his former ease among his family.
terra: His Lord had always seen him, answering the illusion that his worldly course escaped the final return.
terra: The command to glorify the name of the Lord Most High restores the title Pharaoh claimed to its proper bearer and matches the face of the Lord Most High sought by the giver.
terra: The Most High creates and proportions, restating the first half of Moses' account of the Lord in the palace.
terra: He determines and then guides, bringing measure and guidance together just as the section's giver-Creator makes the road fit.

luna: The section's night-path scene turns a warning into a sign for the attentive; this command to remind if the reminder benefits supplies the same admonitory stance. | terra: The command is to remind wherever reminder benefits, introducing the warning that separates the hearers in the following ayat.

luna: The section says the warning is a guide for the one who fears; this verse says the reminder will be heeded by the one who fears, directly identifying the responsive listener. | terra: The one who fears will take the reminder, tying responsiveness to the fear that keeps a person from fire.

luna: The section says the heedless one ignores the warning and enters the Fire; this verse sets the most wretched person against the fearful listener as the one who avoids the reminder. | terra: The most wretched person avoids the reminder, the exact contrary course of the hearer who turns aside from the fire itself.

luna: The section's heedless person plunges into the blazing Fire; this verse gives the avoider of reminder the great Fire as his outcome. | terra: That wretched person enters the greatest fire, directly linking refusal of warning to entry into flame.

luna: The section contrasts the Fire with the saved person's contentment; this continuation says the one in it neither dies nor lives, specifying the lasting condition on the warned-against path. | terra: Within it he neither dies nor lives, specifying the condition reached by the one who entered rather than read the fire as a sign.

luna: The section links giving and purification with being kept clear of the Fire; this verse says the one who purifies himself prospers, the other path's direct counterpart. | terra: Success belongs to the one who purifies himself, corresponding to wealth given in order to grow in purity.

luna: The section joins giving to a face sought for God's sake; this verse associates the successful person's purification with remembering the Lord's name and prayer, extending the image from hand to devotion. | terra: He remembers his Lord's name and prays, giving the successful course its orientation toward the Lord Most High.

luna: The section depicts the miser's refusal as a preference for immediate possessions; this verse states directly that people prefer the nearer life (تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا). | terra: People instead prefer the nearer life, naming the temporal preference behind clutched wealth and worldly royal height.

luna: The section's giver seeks an enduring divine reward beyond worldly repayment; this verse says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, explaining that choice. | terra: The Hereafter is better and more enduring, explaining why wealth and rule cannot support their owner at the fall.
terra: Other faces on that Day are humbled, reversing the radiant faces produced by protected, God-directed striving.
terra: They have labored and exhausted themselves, showing striving whose direction yields weariness rather than the رضى of 88:9.
terra: They enter a scorching fire, the low outcome opposed to the lofty garden of 88:10.
terra: Faces on that Day are radiant, matching the section's face disclosed after darkness and protected from the frowning Day.
terra: Those faces are pleased with their striving, directly joining the surah's diverse striving to its final رضى.
terra: They are in a lofty garden, bringing pleased striving, the opened face, height, and garden into the same sequence.

luna: The section separates bounty from a human claim to favor; this verse depicts a person taking abundance as proof that his Lord honored him, exposing the mistaken worldly reading of wealth. | terra: When the human receives expansive provision, he calls it his Lord's honoring, exposing the mistaken equation of received wealth with true elevation.

luna: The section sets the wealthy holder beside the giver; this verse shows the same person treating reduced provision as humiliation, the opposite mistaken reading of God's test. | terra: When provision is measured tightly, he calls it humiliation; the following failures toward orphan and needy show why wealth is not the measure of height.

luna: The section's righteousness is measured by giving, not merely possession; this verse says the wealthy fail to honor the orphan, naming the neglect behind their self-assessment. | terra: The rebuke that people do not honor the orphan gives the first concrete failure behind their claim that wealth itself is honor.

luna: The section makes feeding part of the giving path; this verse says the people do not urge one another to feed the poor, an exact contrary social act. | terra: They do not urge feeding the needy, directly reversing the face-seeking feeders whom God shields.

luna: The section opposes giving to grasping wealth; this verse says they consume inheritance greedily, showing possession become appropriation. | terra: They consume inheritance voraciously, presenting the grasping relationship to wealth that accompanies failed giving.

luna: The section's miser holds wealth as though it sufficed; this verse names their intense love of wealth, exposing the attachment behind withholding. | terra: They love wealth with intense love, the attachment from which the section's miser expects self-sufficiency.
terra: Hell is brought into view on that Day and the human remembers too late, bringing warning-fire and recognition together after the wealth rebukes.
terra: He wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, the regretful opposite of wealth given beforehand for God's face.

luna: The section ends on contentment after the night gives way to an opened face; this verse addresses the tranquil soul and calls it back to its Lord. | terra: The contented soul is directly addressed, giving the section's final رضى an inward bearer.

luna: The source section's final word is رَضِيَ in 92:21; this verse's رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً develops the same satisfaction as both the servant's contentment and God's approval. | terra: It returns to its Lord pleased and pleasing, joining return, mutual approval, and the Lord toward whom the face was directed.

luna: The section's saved person reaches the Lord's favor; this continuation invites that soul among God's servants, giving belonging as part of the reward. | terra: It is invited among God's servants, the saved company opposite the companion found in Hell.

luna: The section contrasts the Fire with the seeker's final contentment; this verse ends the tranquil-soul passage with entry into the Garden, the destination that completes that contrast. | terra: It is invited into God's garden, placing satisfaction at the entrance to the garden-side outcome.

luna: The section says God provides guidance and people take divergent paths; this verse says the human being has been shown the two roads, making divergence the starting point for the following ascent and outcomes. | terra: God shows the human being the two elevated ways, a particularly close counterpart to the section's road dividing before its walkers.

luna: The section's cliff-edge and path imagery meets this verse's difficult ascent (الْعَقَبَةَ), a demanding course rather than mere outward direction. | terra: The person nevertheless does not undertake the steep ascent, turning the moral choice into the section's concrete contrast of height and descent.
luna: The section's steep edge and descent into Fire make the ascent image legible; this verse asks what the difficult ascent is, introducing the concrete deeds in the next lines.

luna: The section cites freeing necks as a mark of goodness; this verse names freeing a neck (فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ) as the first act of the difficult ascent. | terra: The steep ascent is defined first as freeing a neck, meeting the section's use of 2:177 to place release in the giving hand.

luna: The section joins spending with care for people; this verse adds feeding on a day of hunger as part of the upward path. | terra: Feeding on a day of severe hunger makes the difficult upward road an act of provision rather than an image of height alone.

luna: The section's righteousness includes support for vulnerable people; this line specifies an orphan near of kin among those fed on the ascent. | terra: The orphan of near relation identifies one recipient of the feeding by which the steep way is climbed.

luna: The section's giving path includes the needy; this line specifies a poor person in misery as another recipient on the ascent. | terra: The destitute person in misery identifies the low human condition toward which the giver's hand reaches.

luna: The section has the believer use the warning as guidance and follow a protective path; this verse adds mutual exhortation to patience and mercy as the way's communal conduct. | terra: Faith, mutual patience, and mutual mercy make such givers companions of the right, completing the section's road according to the character of its walkers.

luna: The section sets giving and piety on one path and withholding on another; this verse calls the people of that demanding, merciful path companions of the right. | terra: Those who climb through faith and giving are named companions of the right, turning the split path into a final side.

luna: The section's rejected warning ends in Fire; this verse gives the opposite group the name companions of the left after the ascent passage's deeds. | terra: Those who reject God's signs become companions of the left, the opposite side reached after the same two elevated ways are shown.

luna: The section's denier enters the blazing Fire; this verse says the companions of the left are enclosed in a Fire, closing the path-parable with the matching outcome. | terra: A fire closed over the rejecters completes the opposite road from freeing and feeding to confinement in flame.

luna: The section pairs night that covers with day that appears; this verse swears by the day as it displays, repeating the disclosure side of that image in a passage about the soul's moral outcome. | terra: The oath by the day when it discloses brightness closely repeats the section's day opening what the covering night hid.

luna: The section's opening night veils the course of human striving; this paired oath names the night as it covers (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا), repeating the concealment image before the passage turns to purification and failure. | terra: The oath by the night when it covers closely repeats the covering movement from which the section's road scene begins.
terra: The proportioned soul follows the paired night and day, linking cosmic alternation to a creature made fit.
terra: The soul is shown both its corruption and its taqwa, placing the section's divided moral roads within the walker.
terra: Success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, corresponding to the giver whose wealth-giving seeks purification.
terra: Failure belongs to the one who buries the soul, the downward reversal of purification and disclosed light.
terra: The Lord promises to give until the addressee is pleased, joining divine giving to the same future رضى that closes surah 92.
terra: Enduring gardens, God's pleasure with the faithful and theirs with Him, and fear of the Lord all meet in one reward, tightly joining رضى, garden, and protective fear.
terra: The person whose scales are heavy begins the secure outcome of measured striving.
terra: He is in a pleasing life, joining moral weight to رضى rather than to the weight of possessions.
terra: The person whose scales are light begins the reversed outcome, where apparent worldly weight proves empty.
terra: His refuge is an abyss, a direct counterpart to the section's cliff and downward fall.
terra: The abyss is identified as a fiercely hot fire, joining fall and fire in the shortest possible sequence.

luna: The section says worldly wealth will not avail the person who falls; this verse depicts the one who amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, the possession pattern behind that failure. | terra: The condemned person amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, giving the section's clutched and enveloping wealth a recognizable human posture.

luna: The section shows the miser's held wealth failing him; this verse states his false belief that wealth will make him last forever, exposing why he clings to it. | terra: He supposes his wealth has made him immortal, the illusion exposed when wealth cannot avail at the fall.

luna: The section's warning ends in a plunge into Fire; this verse says the wealth-counter will be thrown into the Crusher, enacting that fall. | terra: He is to be cast into the Crusher, supplying a downward end to the wealth he treated as enduring support.
luna: The section's fire image carries both warning and consequence; this question introduces the description of the Crusher that follows.

luna: The section contrasts guiding fire at a distance with the Fire entered by the heedless; this verse identifies the Crusher as God's kindled Fire. | terra: The Crusher is identified as God's kindled fire, completing the movement from accumulated wealth to being thrown into flame.

luna: The section says the other Fire reaches the one who plunges in; this verse says the Crusher penetrates to the hearts, making its inward reach explicit. | terra: That fire rises over hearts, making punishment attach inwardly as the heated treasure attaches to bodies in the section.

luna: The section's rejected one is enclosed in the Fire; this verse says the Fire is closed over them, reinforcing the image of no escape. | terra: The kindled fire is closed over the wealth-counter and his kind, reversing the open road and matching the enclosed fire at the end of the steep-path passage.

luna: The section contrasts an open sign-fire with entered punishment; this final image of extended columns completes the Crusher's enclosing scene. | terra: Its extended columns specify the enclosure's structure, completing the fate of the person who treated accumulated wealth as support.
terra: The question identifies the person who denies judgment, beginning a short sequence in which denial becomes refusal of care for the vulnerable.

luna: The section makes feeding and care part of righteousness; this verse describes the opposite action of harshly repulsing the orphan. | terra: That denier drives away the orphan, making rejection of the final account visible as a hand that repels rather than gives.

luna: The section includes feeding others for God's face; this verse condemns failing even to urge the feeding of the poor, reversing that hand-to-mouth scene. | terra: He does not urge feeding the needy, the direct behavioral reverse of those who feed solely for God's face.
luna: The section says outward orientation alone is not goodness; this verse begins a warning against prayer without its moral substance.
luna: The section distinguishes a true reminder from disregard; this verse describes prayer performed heedlessly, an outward act detached from attention.
luna: The section's giver acts without seeking thanks or return; this verse condemns people who act to be seen, the contrary motive.
luna: The section contrasts open-handed giving with hoarding; this verse ends by condemning those who withhold even small assistance.
terra: A condemned man's wealth and earnings do not avail him, a terse parallel to wealth failing at the instant of ruin.
terra: He will enter a flaming fire, placing that failed wealth directly beside the act of entering the blaze.
